newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Saddam at 60, a survivor in firm control of Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Saddam at 60, a survivor in firm control of Iraq.

text.p: Saddam Hussein marks his 60th birthday next Monday from his strongest position since the Gulf War, celebrating in Iraq with an elaborate party and abroad by thumbing his nose at the United States.

More statues and portraits of the man who has held power for more than a quarter century will be unveiled, adding to thousands that already remind Iraqis the crushing defeat of his 1990 invasion of Kuwait and years of sweeping trade sanctions have failed to undermine his control.

The annual birthday celebrations at his hometown of Tikrit, part of a personality cult that includes portraits of Saddam holding the scales of justice and a giant sculpture of his hands grasping crossed swords, will be larger than ever this year.
"Iraqis will renew their pledge of loyalty to his Excellency President Saddam Hussein...under whose leadership eternal and courageous feats were realised," said the official al-Qadissiya newspaper.
Internationally, the return of some Iraqi oil to world markets after more than six years and a fraying of the coalition that drove his troops from Kuwait, have emboldened Saddam.

When the United Nations Security Council reacted ambiguously this month to Iraq sending a plane with Moslem pilgrims to Mecca in apparent violation of a ban of Iraqi international flights in force since Iraqi troops seized Kuwait in August 1990, Saddam was quick to test the limits.

With state-run media gloating at the U.S. failure to secure a strong Security Council reaction, exactly a week before his birthday Saddam sent helicopters to southern Iraq where the United States has barred Iraqi flights since 1992.
Washington complained of Saddam's abuse of religion, since the helicopters officially were to pick up pilgrims returning from Mecca, but could do little else.
"The U.S. failed drastically," the newspaper al-Iraq said of U.N. support. "It seems it does not want to swallow its defeat and the deterioration of its standing."
The erosion of backing for Washington's anti-Saddam policy has been gradual over the years, with foreign diplomats quietly resuming operations and a steady trickle of businessmen.

Since the oil-for-food deal with the United Nations began in December -- allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil in a six-month period to buy humanitarian needs -- a desire for business as normal has become open. There is increasing foreign fatigue with measures that isolated Iraq from the world but failed to cause the political change in Baghdad many predicted.
This month Iraq's parliament ratified a deal with Russia to develop the Qurna oilfield in southern Iraq, which the state press said included a Russian commitment to spend $200 million.

Foreign firms have long wanted to get at Iraqi oil reserves, second in the world only to Saudi Arabia, but previous deals touted by Baghdad had appeared to delay any active role until after the lifting of a U.N. ban on trade and investment in Iraq.

Those U.N. sanctions can only be lifted after the United Nations Special Commission on Iraq, UNSCOM, says Iraq no longer has weapons of mass destruction or the ability to produce them. Washington maintains even that would not end sanctions.

But after six years of work, UNSCOM head Rolf Ekeus believes Iraq is still concealing weapons or at least information. The task looks set to outlast Ekeus -- he plans to leave his post in a few months.

Saddam is a survivor. He rose through Iraq's plots, coups and assassinations to become the official number two -- and strongman behind President Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr -- in 1969. A decade later he brushed him aside and formally took the presidency.

He then launched a 1980-88 war with Iran, abruptly returning the meagre gains two years after the truce in a futile bid to strengthen his position against the U.S.-led coalition that challenged his annexation of Kuwait. His defeat in the subsequent Gulf War left Iraq's infrastructure in ruins and the country under the toughest U.N. sanctions ever enforced.

His intense personal security became even more formidable. He has not given an interview to a Western reporter since the Gulf War, his whereabouts are never disclosed and he does not even attend his own public birthday celebrations.

That caution, rooted in his own path to power, shows that an end to his rule could come swiftly from an assassin's bullet. His eldest son Uday remains in hospital after a still-murky shooting last year.

But as Saddam holds his usual personal birthday party of children singing his praises inside a well-guarded palace -- where security is controlled by his other son Qusay -- he must be contemplating the growing prospect of many more years as leader of Iraq.
